items.summary_1line: Long-horizon terminal tasks are used to evaluate and train agents. Human-curated datasets are scarce, so many synthesis methods have emerged. They usually measure the length of a task by the turns a model needs to pas...

items.title: One Run Is Not Enough: A Monte Carlo Protocol for Evaluating LLM Reliability on Data Science Tasks
items.summary_1line: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise for automating data science workflows. Benchmarks such as DataSciBench (2026) and StatQA (2024) have advanced the evaluation of their capabilities across data science an...
items.editor_note: Argues a single run is insufficient and proposes a Monte Carlo reliability protocol for data science tasks.

editorial.tldr: Late-October arXiv papers framed long-horizon agent work as an evaluation problem, with benchmarks for continual learning and web search alongside new critic, memory and multi-agent methods. On Nov 1 a paper questioned whether long-horizon terminal benchmarks actually measure depth.
editorial.whats_new: A Nov 6 paper argues one run is not enough and proposes a Monte Carlo protocol for measuring LLM reliability on data science tasks, following new consumer-task (LifeVal) and multilingual tool-use (τ-bench-LILT) benchmarks.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent benchmark scores are only as trustworthy as the task design and run count behind them: depth, language coverage and run-to-run variance all change what a number means for your deployment.
editorial.take_for_builders: Rerun your internal agent evals several times and report the spread rather than a single score, and add non-English tool-use cases before trusting an English-only benchmark result.

status.detail: Research is shifting from adding long-horizon benchmarks to questioning their depth, language coverage and single-run reliability.
